findings.text: Times are compared via UnixNano(), which is undefined outside roughly years 1678–2262. For example, `Greater(t, time.Now(), time.Time{})` or `Less(t, time.Time{}, time.Now())` overflows the zero time, so the result is wrong and a correct assertion can fail. `Before`/`After`/`Compare` should be used instead.

Only obj1 is checked with CanConvert(timeType). obj2 is converted unchecked, and the Greater/Less callers only check that both values are the same Kind (struct). `Greater(t, time.Now(), struct{X int}{1})` therefore makes `obj2Value.Convert` panic instead of failing the assertion cleanly.

`Value.CanConvert` needs Go 1.17 or later. Any module that still supports an older Go version will not build. Also, a time.Time-typed obj1 compared with a non-time obj2 takes the same unguarded path as the finding above.

1.reason: Only obj1 is checked with CanConvert(timeType). obj2Value.Convert(timeType) runs unguarded, and the callers only require both values to share the struct Kind, so a non-convertible struct as obj2 makes reflect panic instead of failing the assertion.

2.reason: reflect.Value.CanConvert was added in Go 1.17, so this breaks builds for a module that still targets older Go versions (testify's go.mod declared go 1.13; the later fix switched to Type.ConvertibleTo). This is a separate defect from the UnixNano overflow.
